question: Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte (GFF) is an association in Germany that was set up in 2015 and purports to defend supposed fundamental rights. Cases are selected specifically to bring about wide-reaching legal decisions. The association submits constitutional complaints, prepares expert opinions and runs media campaigns.

While it describes itself as non-partisan, the choice of topics and the patterns of arguments used are anchored in an ideological, liberalprogressive fundamental rights discourse. The organisation’s inconspicuous mask recently slipped. It openly acts as an arm of antidemocratic forces, which use any means necessary to impose a ban on the party leading every opinion poll: Alternative für Deutschland (AfD).

To that end, an expert report is currently being prepared, for which former AfD politicians have also been approached to encourage them to make statements criticising the party or provide internal information and documents.

In doing so, the organisation does not act as an independent association, but rather as an active political actor that uses rule of law procedures as a pretext to undermine the democratic representation of a large portion of the population. In view of these developments, it must be ensured that organisations that have such an antidemocratic agenda do not have access to EU funding. 1.
Has GFF ever applied for or received EU funding, including indirect funding by way of third-party organisations?
What mechanisms are in place to ensure that EU funds do not go to organisations that seek to undermine democratic processes or restrict the people’s political representation?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.1.2026) We refer the Honourable member to the answer to question E-002215/20251 in which we confirmed that Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte is not a beneficiary of EU funding neither directly nor indirectly. The organisation did not apply for EU funding. The Commission implements the mechanisms provided in the Financial Regulation2 for the award of funds.
It carries out rigorous selection processes, including several different checks on grant beneficiaries based on objective criteria such as the exclusion criteria or the EU restrictive measures.

The Financial Regulation foresees that entities guilty of grave professional misconduct including incitement to hatred or violence or similar acts that are contrary to EU values and negatively affecting or risking to affect the performance of the legal commitment must be registered in the Early Detection and Exclusion System (EDES) Database and can be excluded from all EU funding for up to three years.

In addition, during implementation, EU funded projects are closely monitored to ensure that they are implemented according to the grant agreement and the description of works. The model grant agreement used by the Commission for granting funds requires that beneficiaries commit to respect EU values during the implementation of the project.

In the event of incorrect implementation n cases of fraud, irregularities, substantial errors or serious breach of contractual obligations including the violation of EU values the grant may be suspended, terminated or reduced and funds may be recovered.
